Newport is a flourishing port, market town, and parliamentary and municipal borough, in the parish of St. Woollos, pleasantly situated on the banks of the river Usk. It is distant by railway from London, 158½ miles ; Bristol (viâ Bristol and South Wales Union Railway), 28 ; Cardiff, 12 ; Swansea, 57 ; Monmouth, 23 ; Chepstow, 17½ ; Pontypool, 8 ; Abergavenny, 17½ ; and Tredegar, 23. It is in the lower division of the hundred of Wentloog, union and county court district of its own name, Bristol district court of bankruptcy, diocese of Llandaff, archdeaconry of Monmouth, and deanery of Newport. Job / Trade: business is also done in timber, bark, slate, and corn. Various other manufactures requiring much capital and labour are largely carried on.

Another source of opulence to the port is ship building, which is conducted to an important extent, the river being peculiarly well adapted for this business, as vessels of almost any burthen can be launched from the dock into deep water. The chief exports are iron and coal, which are sent to all parts of the world. The weekly markets are on Wednesday and Saturday, the former for cattle, sheep, and horses, and the latter for corn, provisions, and the usual articles of consumption. There is also a great market on the third Monday in every month. Fairs are held on Holy Thursday, Whit Thursday (cattle and pleasure), August 15th, first Tuesday after October 10th, and November 6th. The place derives its interest entirely from the rapid growth and great prosperity of its trade, manufactures, and commerce; and the inhabitants look forward with delight to the completion of the Alexandra Docks; and its rise to a status of far greater importance as a port and commercial town than it has ever yet attained, becomes more and more apparent.

COMMUNICATIONS.—The increased facilities both for the conveyance of coal and iron to this port for shipment, and for passenger traffic, tend greatly to its prosperity. Newport has direct communication by means of the Great Western Railway with the metropolis in one direction, and with Milford, thence by packet to the South of Ireland in the reverse direction. The Great Western station is situated in High-street. The narrow-gauge system extending hence to Liverpool, Manchester, and the North of England, is also Great Western property, but is better known as the West Midland Railway. The station of this line is in Mill-street. Here are also the chief offices and locomotive works of the Monmouthshire Railway and Canal Company. This line intersects the Eastern and Western Valleys; the former extends to Pontypool and Blaenavon (from Mill-street station), and the latter to Risca, and thence to Blaina and Nant-y-glo (Dock-street station). The Sirhowy Railway (formerly a tramway used for mineral transit only), was opened for passenger traffic on June 19th, 1865. It forms direct communication between Newport and the great iron districts of Tredegar and Sirhowy, a distance of 23½ miles, although it runs over 9 miles of the Monmouthshire Railway to “Nine Mile Point,” a little beyond Risca. The Newport, Brecon, and Merthyr Tydvil Railway, opened for passenger traffic June 14th, 1865, also runs over that portion of the Monmouthshire between Newport and Bassaleg, and passes through Machen, and will, when completed, form a direct route between Newport and Brecon. In the last session of parliament (1865), an act was obtained for the construction of the Pontypool, Caerleon, and Newport Railway, which will commence at a point near the Pontypool-road junction of the Great Western, and extend viâ Pontnewydd and Caerleon to Newport. This line will run almost parallel to the Monmouthshire for several miles. The coming session of parliament is looked forward to with some interest in this district, for it is expected powers will be applied for to construct a narrow-gauge line from Newport to Cardiff, side by side with the Great Western, which will place the Glamorganshire and Monmouthshire Valleys in communication with one another without break of gauge, and which

Surname: will enable the Midland and London and North Western Companies to compete more successfully for a share of the South Wales traffic to the north and midland counties. Another project is a more direct line from Merthyr and Aberdare to Newport, and, if carried out as proposed, Aberdare will be equi-distant from Newport and Cardiff, Merthyr will be 1 mile nearer Newport than Cardiff, and the Dowlais Iron Works 4 miles nearer. The river Usk is navigable for vessels of large size, and has a very rapid and high tide, and affords every facility for an extensive maritime trade. The steamers of the Bristol General Steam Navigation Company and the New Steam Packet Company, Limited, regularly ply between this port and Bristol; the Cork Steam Ship Company run powerful vessels between Newport and Ireland, and its trade with that country is important.

A handsome stone bridge, erected at a cost of £10,165, crosses the river Usk, consisting of five arches, the span of the centre arch being 70 feet, the two adjoining 62 feet, and the remaining two 55 feet each. It was constructed by Mr. David Edwards, son of the celebrated Edwards, who erected the far-famed bridge of one arch at Pontypridd, in Glamorganshire. This bridge is now being widened, at the expense of the county, to afford accommodation for the amount of traffic continually passing over it. The South Wales Railway also crosses the river by a bridge of scientific construction. The Monmouthshire Canal commences on the western side of the town, having a basin connected with the river Usk. It consists of two branches, which unite at Malpas, and pursues its route parallel to the river Avon by Pontypool to Pontnewynydd, an extent of nearly eleven miles in one direction, and opposite Malpas a branch strikes off parallel to the river Ebbw in a direction to Crumlin bridge, forming a line of more than 11 miles from the junction. The Breconshire Canal forms a communication between Newport and Brecon, by way of Pontypool and Abergavenny, forming a junction with the Monmouthshire Canal 8½ miles from Newport and 1 from Pontypool.

NEWSPAPERS.—There are three weekly newspapers published here: The Monmouthshire Merlin and South Wales Advertiser, by Mr. William Christophers; The Star of Gwent, by Mr. Thomas Williams; and the Newport Gazette, by Mr. W. N. Johns; and Mr. Marshall Owen Scott publishes a Circular and Magazine Monthly. The above are very extensively circulated in this and adjoining counties.

GENERAL ASPECT AND PUBLIC BUILDINGS.—The general aspect of the town is that of decided prosperity, and the improvements that are constantly effected, both with respect to neatness and extent, reflect the highest credit on the inhabitants, and, combined with its local advantages, entitle it to be considered the metropolis of the county. It contains all the usual public buildings for municipal and trading purposes, for education, and for divine worship. The principal street, which extends from Newport bridge to Pillgwenlly, is spacious, and contains many handsome shops, banking establishments, and several good hotels, of which the Westgate, King's Head, and Queen's, are the principal family and commercial houses. Job / Trade: Christchurch is an extensive parish, distant about $2\frac{1}{2}$ miles from Newport, on the Chepstow road, in the Newport union and county court district, diocese of Llandaff, archdeaconry of Monmouth, and deanery of Netherwent (western division). The parish comprises an area of 5757 statute acres.

The church is situated on an eminence, from which a fine view of the Bristol Channel and the surrounding country may be obtained. The living is a vicarage, in the patronage of Eton College, and held by the Rev. Thomas Pope, M.A., and rural dean.

Maindee, in this parish, is a delightful suburb of Newport, and contains many elegant residences, chiefly of merchants, professional gentlemen, &c., having business at Newport. It is situated about a mile from the town, and has, within the last few years, sprung up into a place of importance. The church of St. John the Evangelist is a district church, under the vicar of Christchurch. The Rev. Jas. Newman, B.A., is the curate. There are also places of worship for dissenters. The population in 1861 was 3004.

Postal Regulations.—Mrs. McDaniell, Sub-Postmistress. Letters arrive from Newport and are delivered at 7.0 a.m., and at 3.0 p.m.; dispatched at 7.0 p.m. Money Order Office and Savings Bank open from 9.0 a.m. until 6.0 p.m. Post town, Newport.
